EVERLASTING APPRECIATION
npHE Fraternity owes a debt of gratitude to Earl D. Babst and Theodore
-*- L. Waugh that will be hard to pay. Their long and valuable service
on the Executive Council has been noteworthy in the History of Psi Upsilon
and the present extremely healthy condition of the fraternity is due in
no small way to the efforts of these two noble brothers. It is unfortunate
in cases like theirs that it is not possible for every member of the fraternity
to realize the great amount of work that the Council does so that every
one could thoroughly appreciate how valuable their aid and advise has been.
It is to be hoped that they will continue as ex-ofi5cio members of the
Council for their analytical experienced minds are
really needed in the
running of an
organization constructed as ours is where conservatism with
discretion must be had from well trained men who have reached the posi
tions in life that these two brothers have.
Theodore Leland Waugh has been a member of the Council since 1912,
he graduated from Syracuse University in 1898 with the degree of A.B.
taking his LL.B. in 1902. Until recently he has been Assistant District
Attorney of New York City from which position he has resigned to resume
the practice of law with offices at 350 Madison Ave., New York.
Earl D. Babst was elected to the Executive Council in 1907 and has
served continuously. He is President of the American Sugar Refining Co.
An interesting but brief sketch of his life was given in the January 1922
issue of The Diamond (pp. 82) .
In this modest way we express our appreciation to Brothers Babst
and Waugh, and we hope that they will know that Psi Upsilon holds
them as worthy sons because they have honestly but modestly earned her
real appreciation.

In the afternoon everybody went by motor to Newman's resort at
Saratoga Springs where we were guests of the Theta at a dinner long to be
remembered; the singing of our fine old songs was excellent.
It is to be noted that the conduct of the delegates was entirely ini

occurred, so frequently associated with general fraternity conventions.
On Saturday morning a generous welcome was extended to the del
egates by President Charles A. Richmond of Union College, who greeted
the Convention in person. His words of wisdom were heartily received and
his praise of our grand old mother chapter and the fraternity were in
spiring. Personal presentation of petitions were then made by representatives
of Phi Kappa Chi of Johns Hopkins University, the El Paso Club of
Iowa State University, and the Wranglers of Northwestern University who
were
granted an
opportunity to address the delegates sitting as a committee

The convention then resumed its formal sessions which lasted until
nearly five o'clock with one short recess for luncheon and the taking of
the official convention picture.
The petition of the Pi Upsilon Society of the University of Kansas
again past the convention and will again be referred to the chapters for a
ratification vote. Nineteen of our chapters have taken official favorable
action on our granting a chapter to this society and the representatives
of chapters that have sent undergraduate delegations to Lawrence, Kansas,
to visit Pi Upsilon and the University spoke in praise of their findings.
Those so reporting were John W. Fawcett, Sigma, '22, John Wilson, Theta
Theta, '22, and Frederick L. Worcester, Phi, '22. It is singular that no
delegation or
personal investigation has yet been made to this University
and group without being thoroughly convinced of the wisdom of placing a
chapter there. Brother Wm. L. Burdick, Xi, '02, Vice Chancellor of the
University and Dean of the Law School represented Pi Upsilo^ and he
went home feeling that before another convention Psi Upsilon will be
established at the University of Kansas.
Further expansion beyond the above was very positively and unan
imously opposed.
Two men were elected to the Executive Council to fill the vacancies
caused by the expiration of the terms of Earl D. Babst, Phi, '93 and
Theodore L. Waugh, Pi, '98. Dr. George Henry Fox, Upsilon, '67 and
Charles Phillip Spooner, Rho, '94 being selected to serve for five year terms.
Elsewhere in this issue will be found a few words of appreciation for the
excellent service of the two former members of the Council whose advice

MAJOR THAIN WENDELL MacDOWELL, V.C, D.S.O.
THE photograph published opposite p. 213 was taken at Buckingham
Palace just as His Majesty, King George V., assisted by his Grenadier
Guards, finished the ceremonies of investing Brother MacDowell of the "Nu"
with the Victoria Cross and the Distinguished Service Order.
The Victoria Cross is the highest honor granted by the British Empire
for valour in the enemy's presence. During the four years the Canadians
were engaged in the late war, they only received 58 of these coveted medals,
and of this number, twenty-two were awarded to men for signal acts of
devotion in which they lost their lives. Thanks be. Brother MacDowell
wasn't one of these, but his escape seems marvelous even when one takes
the censored account of his actions which the authorities published in Lon
don Gazette No. 30122, p. 5702. At Vimy Ridge, France, on
9/13-4-17.
For most conspicuous bravery and indomitable resolution in the face of the
enemy; by his initiative and courage he and two runners captured a ma
chine gun nest which barred the way of an advance. MacDowell rushed
the strongpoint and killed or put out of action the crews of two machine
guns. When his runners came up, although he was wounded, he descended
into an
underground shelter and captured two officers and seventy-five men.
He sent back one runner in charge of these and with the other he held the
captured position for five days, in spite of intense enemy activity, until
finally his battalion succeeded in relieving him.
The Distinguished Service Order is a British Naval and Military Order
of distinction by which instances of meritorious or distinguished service in
war are rewarded. Like other military honors, it is never awarded unless
the recipient has shown his worth in a long series of gallant actions and an
unbroken record of good conduct. The particular action selected for con
ferring the companionship of the order on Brother MacDowell as given by
the censors in London Gazette No. 29898, at page 454, is: "10-1-17 for con
spicuous gallantry in action. He led his company against an enemy posi
tion with great courage and initiative, captured three machine guns and 50
prisoners. Later, although wounded, he remained at his post and greatly
assisted in the success of the operations."
As an
undergraduate, Brother MacDowell played on Toronto Varsity
Senior teams in football, ice hockey, lacrosse and baseball. He graduated
with honors and at present is the general manager of the Eastern Canada
Motors, Limited, at Hull, Quebec. His great record has not had any detri
mental effect on our brother's charming personality. He is the same mod
est, retiring chap whom we all knew at Collie. The only ill effect he
experiences is a slight stoppage in his speech which has resulted from his
having been shellshocked, but he is too popular to be allowed to remain a
bachelor much longer, so we confidently expect that in self-defence he will
soon be forced to overcome that disability.

PSI UPSILON IN JAPAN
Ernest W. Clement, Omega, '80
Tokyo, March 3, 1922.
IT
IS possible that the brothers in America or elsewhere will be interested
in a few notes concerning Psi Upsilon in Japan. Here our noble fra
ternity has always had a worthy representation, good in numbers and in
names, good in quantity and in quality. Ever since I came to Japan, almost
35 years ago, I have tried to keep track of the Psi Upsilon brothers here.
I have also been able to get more or less information concerning other fra
ternities; and, while I have not succeeded in getting full details, I know
this much, that Psi Upsilon has always maintained first place. Never has
any other fraternity equalled our record here. Let me give a few points
concerning the past and the present of Psi Upsilon in Japan.
Past
It seems proper, from every point of view, to mention first the late
Rev. D. C. Greene, D.D., Zeta, '64. He was the pioneer Congregational
missionary to Japan; and throughout his long service here he constantly
maintained a high rank in the estimation of both Japanese and foreigners.
He was a real missionary-statesman, or statesman-missionary, whichever
we choose to call him. He was the leader of his mission and his fellowmissionaries.
Next, in chronological order, comes a Japanese brother, the late Noriyuki Kojima [Kozima], Chi, '79, who was
professor of drawing and head
of the English department in the First Higher School, Tokyo. He and the
writer were colleagues for several years; and we had the pleasure once of
welcoming Brother Minshall, Chi, '82.
One of the most prominent of Psi Upsilon alunmi in Japan was the
late Nicholas W. Mclvor, Beta Beta, '82. He was U. S. Consul-General at
Yokohama for several years and was one of the best officials ever in the
consular service here. After he retired from that service, he practiced law
in Yokohama. And let me add here, that a son, Carlisle C. Mclvor, is also
a Psi Upsilon, Beta Beta, '17.
The class of '80 of the Beta Chapter holds the honor of having had two
representatives in Japan: Sidney C. Partridge, D.D., who for several years
was
Bishop of the Kyoto Diocese; and Doremus Scudder, D.D., who was
for a short time a Congregational missionary at Niigata and recently was
Pastor of the Union Church, Tokyo.
Morton D. Durming, Gamma, '96, was for many years a teacher of Eng
lish in Doshisha, a Christian university in Kyoto.

pass by the first one, who is the writer. The second is Tomisaburo Glover,

The next four are Japanese brothers: Ayskeh Kabayama,* Xi, '89, who
is one of the leading men of the Mitsui Company, which represents another
multi-millionaire family, of the same name as the company; Baron Naibu
Kanda, Gamma, '79, English scholar, educator, and member of the House
of Peers; Manzo Kushida, Tau, '90, head of the banking department and a
director of the above-mentioned Mitsubishi Company (a member of the
Japanese business men's party recently in the U. S. A.) ; and Masao Matsukata, Tau, '94, president of the Naniwa Bank, recently amalgamated with
the Fifteenth Bank, or Nobles' Bank. Right here let me add that Brother
Kabayama is a son of the late Admiral Kabayama, who has been Minister
of the Navy and Minister of Education; while Brother Matsukata is a son
of Marquis Matsukata, the only surviving member of the original group of
Genro, or Elder Statesmen.
The eighth brother is S. W. Ryder, Beta, '09, a missionary of the
Dutch Reformed Church; and the ninth one is another Japanese brother,
Inajiro Tajiri, Beta, '78, ex-Mayor of Tokyo.
The next three on the list are missionaries: Rev. Henry Topping,
Omega, '81, Baptist, just now home on furlough; Rev. Herbert Welch,
D.D., LL.D., Xi, '87, Bishop of the Methodist Episcopal Church for Japan
and Korea; and Rev. N. C. Whittemore, Delta, '90, Presbyterian, in Korea.
The thirteenth Psi Upsilon brother is H. R. Wilson, Beta, '06, who
has recently come to Tokyo as Counsellor of the American Embassy.
Summary
It will be seen from these lists of past and present Psi Upsilon broth
ers in Japan that the fraternity has been and is well represented in every
walk of life. Business circles, consular and diplomatic service, educational
circles and missionary work have all had honorable Psi Upsilon representa-

PSI UPSILON HERALDRY
PSI
UPSILON HERALDRY. Did you ever
stop to think about it? Did
you ever know the why and the wherefore of those "mystic symbols"
set forth on both the national and chapter coat of arms. Many of us have
given little thought to these symbolic emblems, many of us have had but
a small conception of the completeness and uniformity of the system em
ployed. We take so many things for granted in this hurried age that we
often fail to see the beauty of detail.
It will possibly be interesting, no doubt enlightening to some, to con
sider briefly the development of our Psi Upsilon "Family Tree" as inter
preted through our coat of arms.
In the first place heraldry had its early development when shields
were used for defense. From history we learn that in the early ages indi
viduals, families and tribes adopted various emblems and symbols to serve
as their particular marks of distinction. That they might be easily identi
fied in battle, these marks were placed on
ensigns and shields. The Greeks
and Romans and other early nations assigned various emblems to indi
viduals and even to their deities. The owl was the emblem of Minerva,
Goddess of Wisdom. When heraldic emblems were first used there was little
or no definite scheme for the adaption or arrangement of the symbols.
Later in England there were certain legislative enactments which brought
heraldry to a
systematic and scientific basis. The color schemes, designs,
the symbols, metals and furs used on the shields originally were
pur
ported to be suggestive of deeds of valor, ideals or aims. We also find
that an individual or family who gave allegiance to another, often adopted
the coat of arms of the latter with some alterations to show respect and
possibly class distinction.
In addition to being used by families and individuals, armorial bear
ings came to be used by towns and cities, corporations, hotels and other
institutions such as colleges, universities and societies. In America this
general use has become more
popular than the use of coats of arms for the
individual. The use of armorial bearings which most nearly conforms to
the historic and established principles and codes, has been developed by
the various college fraternities. An article, which appeared some time
ago in Banta's Greek Exchange, and to which the writer is indebted for
considerable of the above data, sets forth clearly and in a manner most
interesting, the systems adopted by almost all the American fraternities.
Nearly all of them have but one national coat of arms without any special
emblems or symbols for the various chapters. Only a few have a system
of employing one national coat of arms and a similar yet distinctive device
for each chapter. Among these are Delta Kappa Epsilon, Beta Theta Pi
and our own Psi Upsilon.

Back in 1892 Brothers Albert P. Jacobs, Phi, '73, Karl P. Harrington,
Xi, '82 and George B. Penny, Chi, '85, acting as a Psi U. Heraldry Com
mittee, prepared and presented a
report outlining the system of heraldry
which was adopted by our Convention of 1894. This system is so
simple,
so uniform and the principles of heraldry are foUwed so
pleasingly, we can
well be thankful that those "who bore the honors of the past" performed
their tasks and established the system with such a
thorough knowledge
of the subject. As was natural they used the ancient symbols upon our
cherished diamond and the emblem peculiar to the various chapters fur
nished the material for the various designs. They sought to utilize the old
insignia and did so most effectively. "The clasped hands are there." The
entire system of devices employing, as it does, historic emblems and prin
ciples, presents a desired significance "to mortals who taste not our bless
ings" and holds many a hidden and treasured meaning for those who
"know how hearts expand."
The national coat of arms, with the gold letters and clasped hands on a
black field, with tressures or small border lines rimning around the shield,
plainly typifies that which "binds our hearts in one." The crest, consisting
of an owl surmounting Roman fasces (a bundle of rods bound by a red
thong and containing a ax with blade projecting) probably needs no fur
ther explanation. Our colors appear, and the silver griffin on each side,
typifies to those familiar with heraldic emblems, watchfulness and strength.
The coat of arms of the various chapters all have a
similarity readily
noticed by comparison. There is a consistent and harmonious scheme which
would have been impossible had each chapter employed a device with
out thought of the common spirit or identity of the other chapters. The
owl for die crest of each, the mottos on uniform scrolls, the shield of each
chapter uniformly present, the emblems of the fraternity together with
symbols appropriate for each chapter. The acorn of the Theta, the dexter
(right) hand of the Delta, the chevron of the Beta and the key of the
Kappa, et cetra, expresses in heraldic language certain ideals or aspira
tions or typifies incidents relating to the founding of that particular chapter.
Could any system of designs, adaptable to the ornamentation of chap
ter houses, lodge rooms or to the printing of fraternal publications, chap
ter stationery, or for use with the chapter lists appearing in the college
annals, be more harmonious or more appropriate? To the casual observer
our coat of arms may have but little significance. Yet to those who know
that "holier union than chivalric circle" does it not make us a little more
proud and a little more glad that we were "tenderly put through" when,
with understanding, we translate the markings and insignia of Psi Upsilons
armorial bearings? We cannot but feel grateful to those brothers who

208 The Diamond of Psi Upsilon
devised, perfected and instituted such a
complete and carefully planned
symbolic system.
Just as the never-to-be-forgotten songs we
sing tell of our fraternal
aims and ideals, so do our coat of arms, national and chapter, symbolize
our aspirations and achievements.
A few of the younger chapters, founded in recent years are without
coat of arms. Attention should be given these by the proper parties and
suitable devices conforming to the general scheme should be adopted with
out delay.
